newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian troops chase fleeing opposition force.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian troops chase fleeing opposition force.

text.p: Hundreds of Cambodian government troops supported by rocket and artillery fire chased opposition forces west along Route 6 about 50 km (30 miles) outside Siem Reap and the Angkor Wat temple complex on Sunday, eyewitnesses said.
Reporters on the scene saw heavily armed government foot soldiers streaming along the highway, and through the rice paddies on either side, in pursuit of a rapidly retreating adversary.

Sunday's government advance was slowed but not halted by a downed bridge over the River Plang. The bridge was blown up on Friday by retreating opposition troops, comprised of Khmer Rouge leftist guerrillas and soldiers loyal to First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh, who was ousted from his position one week ago.

Early Sunday morning, four government tanks forded the river which was swollen to chest height by heavy seasonal rain. Infantry troops clambered over the bridge's splintered planks and linked up with their tanks west of the river.

By 10 a.m. (0300 GMT) on Sunday, the government column had advanced more than five km (three miles) west of the river. Rockets and 122-mm artillery fire was pounding suspected opposition positions five km further down the road.
"Our plan for today is to go as far and as fast as we can," said Vong Kasal, a government commander at the front.
"How far we can get today depends on the situation. We are worried about mines on the road. They (opposition forces) are retreating so fast we are having a difficult time catching them."
Two tanks spearheaded the government advance led by soldiers sweeping the road for mines as the infantry fanned out on either side of the highway through rice paddies dotted with sugar palms.
The only sounds were the crackle of the commander's radio and the sound of shells whistling overhead and hitting down the road.
Government troops said they expected to catch the retreating opposition forces by late afternoon, but their optimism seemed unwarranted. Neither side has evinced much appetite for a real fight.

There was no small arms or machine gun fire on Sunday, a sure sign that the two forces had yet to come close. Observers here expected the opposition forces to continue withdrawing west toward Khmer Rouge positions, with government troops following them but at a safe distance.

Doctors at area hospitals said there had been only five government casualties in a week of fighting here, another indication that the troops might be content to give their political leaders time to work out a compromise before fighting any pitched battles.
As government tanks and infantry moved west, a logistical tail stretched back for many miles east along Route 6 as the army tried to keep its fighting troops supplied.

Army trucks, motorcycles and soldiers on foot hauled artillery shells and metal canisters of 7.62-mm Kalashnikov ammunition to the front, along with sacks of rice, cooking pots and communications gear.

Area villages, which had been virtually deserted on Saturday, including Sor Sdomp and Prey Choup, were bustling with activity a day later as residents flooded back home on the strength of the government's advance. Some families were even returning to the west side of the Plang river, an indicator that the situation outside Siem Reap was stabilising.
Cambodian military police in blue berets were also seen moving into the region to consolidate gains made by army infantry and artillery forces.
"I came back to my home by motorbike this morning and I'm glad to be here with my wife and children and pigs," said Kam, a farmer in Prey Choup just east of the Plang river.
"I think the fighting is gone away from here now. The army has done a good job. I think we are safe."
